title: Emergency Vehicles
strapline: Nee-naw, nee-naw — the fire engine, ambulance and police car racing to help, with a job for everyone.
intent: Children play out helping and rescuing, exploring who keeps us safe and how.
Children make and respond to sounds and signals — sirens, radios, urgent calls for help.
Children build a strong sense of the people who help us and the wider community.
Children cooperate on an urgent shared mission — a fire to put out, someone to rescue, a road to reopen.
Children use number, position and speed as they respond to the emergency.
implementation: Provide fire engines, ambulances and police cars, plus hats, hoses and a phone for 999.
Take the caller's role — 'help, my cat's stuck up the tree!' — and let children mount the rescue.
Model the urgent talk and the radio calls: 'Fire engine to base, we're on our way.'
Give each vehicle a real job and let children choose their role — driver, firefighter, paramedic.
Weave in maths — how many minutes to get there, which route is quickest, count the crew on board.
Talk warmly and truthfully about the real people who help us, and what they do.
Invite the sounds — sirens, alarms, radios — and the difference between loud, urgent and calm-and-safe.
key_questions: Who can we call when there's an emergency, and how?
Which vehicle do we need for this job — and why?
How will your crew put the fire out safely?
Which is the quickest way to get there in a hurry?
How does the paramedic help someone who is hurt?

impact.text: Children play out rescue and helping stories, taking roles and cooperating on the mission.
Children make and answer siren and radio sounds and enjoy the effect on purpose.
Children talk knowledgeably about the people who help us and the community around them.
Children show care and empathy in role — comforting the hurt, reassuring the frightened.
Children use number and position — minutes, routes, crew counts — as they respond.
Children narrate the urgent story with rich vocabulary — siren, rescue, emergency, patient.

enhancements: Fire engines, ambulances and police cars with working (or pretend) sirens.
Firefighter hats, hoses (rope), a first-aid kit and a police radio.
A phone for calling 999 and a clipboard for logging the emergency.
A cat up a tree, a doll to bandage, a wall to rebuild — real jobs to do.
A map or road layout for planning the quickest route.
Photos or a visit from a real fire engine, ambulance or PCSO.
A quiet 'all safe now' zone for the calm after the rescue.

playing_exploring: Children throw themselves into urgent, exciting rescue play.
They explore sounds and signals and the roles of the helpers.
active_learning: Children see the rescue through from the call to the all-clear.
They keep going until the fire is out and everyone is safe.
creating_thinking: Children choose the right vehicle for the job and plan the fastest route.
They invent emergencies and work out, together, how to solve them.
